newsitem.title: INDIA: Striking Indian truckers, government move closer.
newsitem.headline: Striking Indian truckers, government move closer.

text.p: Striking truck owners inched towards a compromise with the Indian government on Tuesday after eight days of deadlock, transport officials said.

"The resumed negotiations with the government in the last two days have taken the shape of draft agreement between the government and the transporters," Chittranjan Dass, secretary general of the All India Motor Transport Congress (AIMTC) said in a statement.
But the draft agreement fell short of the demands of the truck owners that the government drop a planned service tax, he said, adding that efforts were under way to modify the draft agreement.
"Till such time, the indefinite suspension of road transport operations will remain effective all over the country," Dass said.
Industry leaders said production at factories would come to a halt if the strike dragged on for a few more days. Small producers, commodity traders and exporters have been hit hard.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram proposed the tax in the federal budget for the 1997/98 (April-March) financial year.

The budget has been held hostage by a political crisis threatening Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, who faces a confidence vote on Friday. The government has said it cannot rescind the tax as the budget proposal is now before parliament.
"The government can write to the parliamentary panel on finance and suggest withdrawal of the service tax," said S.P. Singh, a spokesman for AIMTC.
The transport body is also protesting against a sharp rise in insurance premiums. The government has offered to refer the rise to a government panel.
The strike has kept at least 2.2 million trucks off the roads. Small transporters who own one or two trucks constitute 93 percent of the country's fleet.

"The biggest problem will be sending out cars," R.C. Bhargava, managing director of Maruti Udyog Ltd, the country's largest car maker, told Reuters when asked about the impact of the strike on his company.
"We will try to keep it going but it may not be to the full extent," Bhargava said. The supply of components has begun to be hit, putting pressure on the cost of production, he said.
The supply of raw materials and transport of finished goods to customers were coming to a standstill, a spokesman for another company said.
Goods have piled up at major ports across the country, exporters said.

"A large number of vessels have stopped calling at the ports. On March 31, the Bombay port was handling 10,500 tonnes of cargo. On April 4, the amount had dwindled to 3,600 tonnes," the Times of India newspaper quoted a Bombay Port Trust official as saying.
